title: For Gaza, a Bloodied Tear at the Corners of My Eyes
intro: Ihab al-Shabatat follows a tear back to the families whose grief brought it to his eye. Two friends might wipe his face, but he asks who will sit with an orphan or help a premature baby breathe. By the end his verses have escaped his keeping and taken to the road like laden she-camels calling for their young.

translation: For Gaza, a bloodied tear at the corners of my eyes.
No physician can cauterise it, no elder charm it away.
1.sharh: Gaza has left him crying blood. He imagines two people trying to stop the flow, a physician with a cautery and a religious healer with a prayer.

translation: It flows when a little girl dies in Gaza
and her father sees her in her last flicker of life.
2.sharh: It is the father's last glimpse that brings on the tear. There is just enough life left in the girl for him to witness its passing.

translation: It flows when a mother in Gaza is scattered
and a child gathers what is left of her.
3.sharh: The child who once fitted into his mother's arms must gather her remains. The verb for gathering ordinarily suggests bringing a family back together.

translation: The child's sobbing fills my ears
and shakes the seven layers of heaven.
4.sharh: The child's voice seems to shake the whole sky. The seven heavens, one above another, give a measure of the distance a sob travels in the listener's imagination.

translation: A mother carrying her child tears my heart apart.
She already knows how far off their next meeting is.
5.sharh: Holding a child is usually a promise of many more embraces. Here the mother already knows this one is a farewell.

translation: My two friends, reproach does my eye no justice.
It never sought tears or the blood in my leg.
6.sharh: He asks two friends to hear his eye's defence. Wanting to weep would be as strange as wanting to shed his own blood, down to the blood in his shin.

translation: My eye was untouched until they came,
tragedies stripped bare in a narrow alley.
7.sharh: He pictures the eye as someone innocent of such sights. The disasters are naked and crowd in through an alley, leaving it nowhere to look away.

translation: My scolding and resistance could not hold them back.
Seduction has a habit of beginning with an embrace.
8.sharh: The disasters approach as though offering an embrace. The sequence from an untouched eye to forced tears turns that apparent tenderness into a violation.

translation: My eye is forced to weep every little while.
My soul has not ransomed it by loosing my bonds.
9.sharh: He would have to give up his own life to release the eye from what it has seen. Ransom and a captive's bonds carry on the image of force.

translation: What joy my wretched heart held flew away.
From the crows came the worst of cawing.
10.sharh: Joy takes wing, leaving crows audible in the empty space. Their harsh calls give the heart an ominous sound of its own.

translation: By God, but for God my soul would have found a way
to guard my eye's sanctuary at the cost of my throat.
11.sharh: His oath gives way to the thought that faith holds him in life. The eye becomes a sanctuary he could otherwise shield from grief only by dying.

translation: My two friends, if my last breath takes pity on me,
who will shield the blood of Gaza's children?
12.sharh: He turns from the little life left in him to the lives of the children. His own pain has someone to feel for it, yet he can name no one to keep their blood from being shed.

translation: If you wipe one tear from my eye, my friends,
who is there for orphans without companions?
13.sharh: He can call on two friends even for a single tear. Counting them brings out the solitude of a child who has lost those who would have wiped its face.

translation: My two friends, if a speck clogs my chest,
how fares a premature child whose breathing is tight?
14.sharh: He can feel what a mote does to his breathing. The poet identifies the child as one of the premature babies in Gaza's hospitals, for whom drawing breath is a struggle.

translation: My two friends, today my show of strength looks foolish.
The clay I am made of was kneaded with tenderness.
15.sharh: The tears disclose what his composure concealed. Tenderness is an ingredient of the clay from which he imagines himself made.

translation: If the cast of my feelings strikes some people as strange,
to lovers' eyes it is the sun.
16.sharh: One person's incomprehensible grief is plain as daylight to someone who loves. Even the measure of understanding is visual, the sun before a pupil.

translation: If a deep-seated trait goes unseen for a time,
the full moon too is hidden in its dark phase.
17.sharh: The gentleness was there even when he seemed composed. Calling the unseen moon “full” asks the reader to remember its familiar face during the dark nights.

translation: My yearning comes of the helplessness of men.
I never thought my verses would seek to leave me.
18.sharh: The distress he cannot remedy has found a voice apart from his own. His verses begin acting like people free to leave with a secret.

translation: I kept my secret well until they rebelled.
They race away spreading word of my tears.
19.sharh: The rebels are his own lines. What he managed to keep off his face travels in the poem faster than he can call it back.

translation: They travel heavy-laden after their cry.
For Gaza they have called as she-camels call.
20.sharh: The verses end as a caravan bearing grief. In Arabic the same family of words names human longing and the cry a she-camel gives for her calf.

1.1.1.head: غَزَّة
1.1.1.meaning: Gaza, the Palestinian city on the Mediterranean that gives the Gaza Strip its name.

1.1.2.meaning: Bloodied or made to bleed. The word is applied to a tear.

1.1.5.head: مَأق
1.1.5.meaning: The inner corners of the eyes, nearest the nose.

1.2.3.meaning: One who cauterises, applying heat to a wound.

1.2.6.head: راقٍ
1.2.6.meaning: People who recite healing prayers, here the elders.

2.2.4-5.head: أَخير رِماق
2.2.4-5.meaning: “The last of her breaths”, the last sign of life.

4.2.4-5.head: سَبع طِباق
4.2.4-5.meaning: “Seven layers”, the seven heavens set one above another in the Quran.

6.2.2.head: اِشتَهى
6.2.2.meaning: To desire. The poet explains that he keeps the final long vowel after lam for the metre.

7.1.3-4.head: بِكر العَين
7.1.3-4.meaning: “Virgin of eye”, someone whose sight is still innocent of such things.

8.2.1.head: دَيدَن
8.2.1.meaning: A settled custom or habitual way of acting.

9.1.2.head: غَصيب
9.1.2.meaning: Under compulsion, as the eye is made to weep.

9.2.2.head: فَدى
9.2.2.meaning: To redeem someone by giving a ransom.

10.2.5.head: نُعاق
10.2.5.meaning: The harsh caw of a crow.

11.2.5.head: تَرقُوَة
11.2.5.meaning: The collarbones, here indicating the base of the throat.

12.1.5.head: حُشاشَة
12.1.5.meaning: The last remnant of life, or the living soul itself.

14.2.2.head: مَخدوج
14.2.2.meaning: A baby born before full term. The poet specifies the premature babies in Gaza's hospitals.

14.2.4.head: خِناق
14.2.4.meaning: The throat. Its tightness here means difficulty breathing.

15.1.5.head: تَجَلُّد
15.1.5.meaning: Assuming an air of fortitude or endurance.

16.2.5.head: حَدَقَة
16.2.5.meaning: Pupils, the dark centres of the eyes.

17.2.6.head: مُحاق
17.2.6.meaning: The dark phase of the lunar month.

18.1.6.head: صَبابَة
18.1.6.meaning: Tenderness and longing strong enough to overcome someone.

19.2.2.head: ذَيع
19.2.2.meaning: The circulation of something previously kept secret.

20.2.4-5.head: حَنين نِياق
20.2.4-5.meaning: “The longing cry of she-camels”, especially when parted from their calves.
